scope: src/rendering.js, src/visualProfiles.js, src/materialLibrary.js, src/environmentMaps.js, src/postGodRayPass.js, src/postSharpenPass.js, src/csShadowRestore.js (render pipeline / post passes / material+visual profiles / env maps), cross-referenced against src/main.js wiring.

findings.title: setLUT3D disposes cache-owned LUT textures, corrupting the per-building LUT cache (use-after-dispose)
findings.description: setLUT3D() unconditionally disposes the previously-active lut3dTexture whenever a new (or null) LUT is set. But the caller in main.js keeps a per-building cache (_lutCacheByBn, line 2080) and re-applies cached textures across building transitions. On a building change setLUT3D(newTex) disposes the OLD building's LUT even though it is still held in _lutCacheByBn. When the player returns to that building, _applyLutForBuilding hits the cache (_lutCacheByBn.has(key), line 2089) and calls setLUT3D() with a texture whose GPU resources were already freed, producing a broken/blank LUT (washed or wrong color grade) and likely a WebGL warning. The setLUT3D(null) path (LUT disabled per settings, line 2084/2105) disposes the active cached texture the same way.
findings.fix: Stop disposing inside setLUT3D since the LUT textures are owned by main.js's _lutCacheByBn (and torn down elsewhere). Remove the `if (lut3dTexture && lut3dTexture.dispose) lut3dTexture.dispose();` block; just reassign lut3dTexture and passes.lut.lut. Alternatively, only dispose when the incoming texture is different AND the outgoing one is not present in any cache (the renderer can't know ownership, so simplest correct fix is: do not dispose). If a leak is feared, dispose cache entries explicitly from main.js teardown only.
findings.risk: Removing the dispose could theoretically leak a LUT texture that was NOT cached, but every LUT path in main.js inserts into _lutCacheByBn before calling setLUT3D, so none are orphaned. No save-compat impact. Keeps build/probes green (pure runtime path).

findings.title: Color-grade pass applies a Reinhard tonemap that double-tonemaps with the renderer's ACES + OutputPass
findings.description: renderer.toneMapping is ACESFilmicToneMapping (main.js line 14732) and the composer chain ends with OutputPass, which re-applies the renderer's tone mapping + sRGB at the end. But makeColorGradeShader's fragment also tone-maps: it multiplies by exposure then does Reinhard `col = col / (col + 0.72)`. So scene HDR is compressed once by the grade pass and again by OutputPass/ACES. Double tone-mapping flattens contrast, crushes/desaturates highlights, and makes the image read less 'punchy' the moment you load. This is the single biggest cheap contrast/saturation win in the pipeline.
findings.fix: Remove the `col = col / (col + vec3(0.72));` line from the grade fragment so the grade pass only does exposure/contrast/saturation/warm-cool/vignette/grain/sharpen, and let OutputPass do the single ACES tonemap. Keep the exposure multiply (it pre-exposes before ACES, which is correct). Verify in one building load that highlights/skylines look richer, not blown; if blown, scale the configure() exposure clamp slightly down. Low code risk, isolated to one shader line.
findings.risk: Image will get noticeably brighter/more contrasty; tuned grade.exposure values (0.78..1.24) may need a small downward nudge to avoid clipping the brightest emissives. No build/probe break (shader string only).

findings.title: God-ray pass computes illuminationDecay per-sample but never weights samples by it (effect mostly discarded)
findings.description: The radial-shaft loop accumulates illuminationDecay *= decay every iteration, but the per-sample contribution is `occ.rgb = min(occ.rgb, samp.rgb)` which ignores illuminationDecay entirely. illuminationDecay is only applied once, as a single scalar (decay^samples ~= 0.81 at 6 samples) to the final shafts. A real radial god-ray (Mitchell) sums per-sample texture contributions weighted by illuminationDecay; here samples are only min'd for occlusion, so the `decay` uniform is essentially a fixed dimming constant rather than a falloff. The shaft look is dominated by `weight` (driven to ~0.52 from reflectionProfile.rays at runtime) and the occlusion min, not the decay falloff it claims to implement.
findings.fix: Either (a) accumulate proper shafts: `vec3 shaftAccum += samp.rgb * illuminationDecay;` and normalize by sample count, then use that instead of the occlusion-min approach; or (b) if the stylized occlusion-min look is intended, drop the per-sample `illuminationDecay *= decay` and the `decay` uniform to remove the misleading dead computation. Only enabled on high/ultra + volumetrics, so visible impact is limited.
findings.risk: Changing to true accumulation alters the shaft look on high/ultra volumetric levels; should be tuned. Removing decay is zero-risk cosmetic cleanup. No build/probe impact.

findings.title: Sharpening is applied twice: inside the color-grade pass and again by the dedicated sharpen pass
findings.description: The color-grade shader applies an unsharp-mask term (`col = mix(col, col + (col - blur), sharpen)`, sharpen ~0.034 high) AND the pipeline adds a separate makePostSharpenPass ShaderPass (strength up to 0.34) later in the chain. Both run when post is enabled, so edges are sharpened twice, which can cause ring/halo artifacts on high-contrast edges and wastes a full-screen pass. configure() already halves grade sharpen when LUT is heavy (line 1004) but never accounts for the dedicated sharpen pass.
findings.evidence:
// grade shader: col = mix(col, col + (col - blur), sharpen);
// plus: sharpenRuntime = makePostSharpenPass(THREE, 0.34); passes.sharpen = new ShaderPass(sharpenRuntime.material);
findings.fix: Pick one sharpener: either set the grade pass's sharpen uniform to 0 when passes.sharpen is enabled (in configure(), guard grade.sharpen by `passes.sharpen && passes.sharpen.enabled ? 0 : value`), or skip adding the dedicated sharpen pass and rely on the grade pass. Reduces a full-screen draw and prevents over-sharpen ringing.
findings.risk: Minor look change (slightly softer edges); could be perceived as less crisp. No build/probe impact.

findings.title: TAA scene-pass path is hard-disabled (useTaaBase=false), leaving an entire TAA configure branch unreachable
findings.description: useTaaBase is a const literal false, so passes.scenePassKind is always 'render' and passes.render is never a TAARenderPass. Consequently the whole TAA configuration block in configure() (taaDesired computation lines 1008-1016 and the `if (passes.render && passes.scenePassKind === 'taa')` block lines 1017-1030) is dead. taaDesired is always false, which also makes the `!taaDesired` SMAA guard a no-op. This is intentional per the comment (TAA trips r170 missing-uniform edge cases on transient VFX materials) but the dead branch and the unused TAARenderPass import/param add noise and risk of future re-wiring confusion.
findings.fix: Leave behavior as-is (TAA is deliberately off), but optionally collapse the dead TAA configure branch to a comment, or keep useTaaBase as a documented kill-switch. No functional change needed; flagging so an editor doesn't 'optimize' the false constant away and accidentally re-enable the unstable TAA path.
findings.risk: None if untouched. Re-enabling TAA would risk the r170 uniform crashes the comment warns about — do NOT flip useTaaBase without revalidating VFX material uniforms.

findings.title: GTAO enable guard tests q !== 'medium-low', a quality tier that never exists
findings.description: passes.gtao.enabled is gated by `q !== 'medium-low'`, but the quality domain in main.js is strictly low/medium/high/ultra (SETTINGS.quality||'high' everywhere). 'medium-low' is never a value, so the guard is always true and never disables GTAO as apparently intended. Harmless today but the guard silently does nothing.
findings.fix: Remove the dead `&& q !== 'medium-low'` clause, or if the intent was to disable GTAO on the 'medium' base quality, change it to `q !== 'medium'` / `q !== 'low'` to match real tiers. Cosmetic correctness only.
findings.risk: If changed to a real tier, GTAO would actually disable on that tier (perf gain, AO loss) — verify intent before changing. Removing the clause is zero-risk. No build/probe impact.

findings.title: God-ray density set by two competing formulas (configure vs tickPhotography) — tick silently wins
findings.description: configure() sets godRayRuntime.uniforms.density from context.godRay (main.js _extrasForRenderStack supplies density = 0.32 + rays*0.48). tickPhotography() then sets the same uniform every frame from extras.godRayDensity (main.js supplies 0.3 + rays*0.45). Because tickPhotography runs each frame after configure, the configure value is immediately overwritten — the configure-time density write is dead and the two formulas disagree (0.32+0.48r vs 0.30+0.45r). Same pattern for weight.
findings.evidence:
// configure(): godRayRuntime.uniforms.density.value = context.godRay.density;  (0.32+rays*0.48)
// tickPhotography(): godRayRuntime.uniforms.density.value = extras.godRayDensity; (0.3+rays*0.45)  // wins every frame
findings.fix: Pick one owner. Easiest: drop the density/weight writes inside configure()'s godRay block (lines 950-953) since tickPhotography already drives them per-frame, or have main.js pass identical formulas in both call sites. Removes a confusing competing-write.
findings.risk: None — final on-screen value is the tickPhotography one, unchanged. Cleanup only.

findings.title: blackFrameSelfTest teardown calls dispose() on lights, which is a no-op for AmbientLight/DirectionalLight
findings.description: The self-test cleanup traverses the scene and calls o.dispose() for o.isLight. Three.js base Light and AmbientLight/DirectionalLight do not implement dispose() (only some lights like RectAreaLight do), so this branch never frees anything. It is harmless (guarded by typeof === 'function') but signals a misunderstanding; the geometries/materials it explicitly disposes are the only real resources, and those are handled.
findings.fix: No action required for correctness. Optionally remove the light-dispose traversal to reduce noise, since the self-test scene's lights are GC'd with the local scene. Lights hold no GPU resources here.

findings.title: getVisualProfile out-of-range fallback uses ((building-1)%8)+1, wrapping into the wrong building's grade
findings.description: VISUAL_TARGETS has 12 entries (buildings 1..12). The fallback for an unknown building is `VISUAL_TARGETS[((building - 1) % 8) + 1]`, which wraps modulo 8, not 12. For building values 9..12 the primary lookup VISUAL_TARGETS[building] succeeds, so the bug is dormant for the normal campaign. But any caller passing building 13+ (e.g. custom maps / demo indices) wraps into buildings 1..8 only and can never reach the 9..12 grades, and building 0 or negative would map to an unexpected slot. The modulo base (8) is inconsistent with the 12-entry table.
findings.fix: Change the modulo base to the table size: `VISUAL_TARGETS[(((building - 1) % 12) + 12) % 12 + 1]` (the extra +12%12 also fixes negatives), or simply `% 12`. Keeps all 12 grades reachable for out-of-range building ids.
findings.risk: Only affects out-of-range building ids; normal 1..12 path unchanged. No save-compat or build/probe impact.

findings.title: applySkyBackgroundFromEquirect mutates the shared HDR equirect mapping and never restores backgroundBlurriness to 0
findings.description: Two small statefulness issues: (1) backgroundBlurriness is only set when blurriness>0 (`if (... && blurriness > 0)`). If a building requests blur and a later building requests blur=0, scene.backgroundBlurriness is never reset, so the previous building's blur persists on the new sky. (2) tex.mapping is forced to EquirectangularReflectionMapping here; the same _equirectByBn texture is the PMREM source, but since PMREM was already generated in loadBuildingEnvironment, mutating mapping post-hoc is benign — flagging only the blurriness latch as a real carry-over.
findings.fix: Always assign backgroundBlurriness when the property exists: `if ('backgroundBlurriness' in scene) scene.backgroundBlurriness = Math.max(0, blurriness || 0);` so a building with blur=0 clears a prior building's blur.
findings.risk: Only changes sky blur carry-over between buildings; visible only if some buildings set skyBlurriness>0 and others 0. No build/probe impact.

findings.title: SSR groundReflector getter is hard-wired to return null, so the SSR pass never gets a real ground reflector
findings.description: createRenderSubsystem is given getGroundReflector:()=>null. tickPhotography then sets passes.ssr.groundReflector from resolveGroundReflectorFn() each frame, which always returns null. The SSR pass code path that mixes a planar ground reflector is therefore never exercised — SSR runs reflector-less. The comment in rendering.js (line 552) anticipated main.js wiring a real getter ('tickPhotography assigns groundReflector each frame') but the getter was left as ()=>null. Either SSR ground reflections are intentionally dropped (then the per-frame reflector plumbing in tickPhotography is dead), or a real getter was meant to be supplied.
findings.evidence: getGroundReflector:()=>null,  // main.js 15281 — rendering.js comment says tickPhotography assigns groundReflector each frame, but source is always null
findings.fix: If planar ground reflections are wanted, wire getGroundReflector to return G.levelData.groundReflector (the wet-floor/marble reflector) when present. If not, this is acceptable but the groundReflector assignment in tickPhotography (rendering.js 754-758) can be removed as dead. Confirm intent before adding a reflector — it has perf cost.
findings.risk: Enabling a ground reflector adds a render cost and could regress perf on high/ultra; only do if a reflector object exists. Leaving as-is is safe. No build/probe impact.
